content:
Here, we have a enat_to_nat! tactic: a stronger enat_to_nat tactic where it will generalise ENat terms before calling enat_to_nat tactic. It has proven quite useful in the Matroid repo when reasoning about Set.encard, Matroid.eRk, Graph.eDegree and etc.

Is there interest in adding this to Mathlib? I would have made a PR myself but I have a very limited understanding of how tactics work. I am not sure I am able to guide it through the PR process.

For context, enat_to_nat is, as currently defined, is incapable of reasoning with, for example, Set.encard S, as it only acts on ENat variables and not ENat terms. enat_to_nat! tries to parse each expression, generalise any ENat "atoms" to ENat variables which enat_to_nat, and probably subsequent omega or lia, can do its magic.

Here is something enat_to_nat!; omega can do but not enat_to_nat; omega cannot. There are more examples at the end of the file linked above.

example {f : ℤ → ℕ∞} {a : ℤ} : 0 ≤ f a := by enat_to_nat!; omega
cc @Vasilii Nesterov as the author of the original enat_to_nat

cc @Heather Macbeth also. She and I wrote this tactic together (she being the one that knows about metaprogramming).

To give a bit more motivation: I believe that ENat is preferable to Nat for a lot of discrete mathematics. Even if the objects itself are finite, minima and maxima are common, and any minimum over a possibly empty set is naturally ENat-valued. For instance, the girth of a graph, which is the length of a shortest cycle if the graph has one, and infinity otherwise. ENat also has the very nice property that suprema and sums are unconditionally well-defined.

In my opinion, it would be great for enat_to_nat to be changed to do what enat_to_nat! does, handling all ENat terms appearing in (in)equalities in the proof state. The current implementation of enat_to_nat! needs work; it would be helpful if a tactic expert could take a look at this.

I also don't know if this is a reasonable suggestion, but my dream would be for lia to work directly with ENat. @Kim Morrison, would this be something that could ever be considered in scope for lia? Here is an example of what I mean: 

example {f : ℤ → ℕ∞} {a b e : ℤ} (h : 2 * f e + f a + f b ≤ f a) :
2 * f a ≤ 3 * f a + f b := by
lia

@Jun Kwon I would suggest adding configuration options to enat_to_nat. Perhaps enat_to_nat +generalize would do your generalization step. Perhaps also enat_to_nat! would be a synonym for enat_to_nat +generalize. This would help integrate it better into the system and be more discoverable.

I could also imagine a generalize_all p : t tactic that locates all terms that match pattern p and have a type that matches pattern t. This way enat_to_nat +generalize could do generalize_all _ : ENat; enat_to_nat.

There are some dependent type issues with generalization that can be annoying if you try to actually generalize all occurrences, where generalization can unnecessarily fail because the result isn't type correct.

It looks like your solution is to parse Exprs and only descend into particular structures, which probably avoids failures, but it doesn't find every ENat atom (e.g. it could be an argument to a function).

It would take some metaprogramming, but one trick that's possible is to lift out all the potential matches as local let definitions, replacing the matches with free variables, and then run Meta.check on the result while enabling a flag to keep track of the set of let definitions are unfolded during typechecking. Everything not in this set can be generalized.

@Kyle Miller As Peter pointed out above, I would hardly call it "my" tactic as I did not write a single line of it: I just know its observed behaviour by using it. Everything you are suggesting sounds amazing! However, I don't have a clue how to write any of that although I would be interested to learn.
